claim: Most machine-proposed lemmas are not useful: across systems, only a minority are both true, new and used. Lemmanaid: 22.6% match human gold lemmas and 23.6% are false; Rabe free-form conjecturing: 12.7% provable-and-new (uniform data), and 49 of 130 theorems later used; template conjecturing: 2 of 10 proved lemmas used in its running example; QuickSpec precision under 1% on Octonions.
agent_test: At equal tokens, log for each lemma the agent proposes: true? new? used in the final proof? Report the used fraction and cost per used lemma; compare against a no-lemma baseline.

claim: A cheap filter stage (compile or type-check, trivial-check, truth test by counterexample or tests, judge) removes a large share of raw candidates before costly proving. MathlibLemma keeps 4,028 of 9,148 proposals (44%); Hipster, QuickSpec and Lemmanaid all use test or counterexample filters.
agent_test: Add a cheap falsification step (small-case check or counterexample search) before any proof attempt on a proposed lemma. Measure tokens saved per useful lemma at equal total tokens.

claim: LLM judges for lemma quality are lossy: of 53 judge-rejected MathlibLemma candidates, 46% were actually valid, and the judge dropped 30-37% of raw candidates. Gap search: a different task (research ideas) shows LLM judges near human-human agreement but low (53.3% vs 56.1%).
agent_test: Sample rejected lemma candidates and verify them by tool; estimate the judge false-negative rate on our own tasks before trusting it as a gate.

claim: Conjecturing helps most when it is a bridge toward a specific goal that the base prover cannot reach. Vampire went from 7 to 25 of 50 TIP problems with QuickSpec lemmas; template conjecturing gave +40 points on Prod; chained conjecturing raised HOL Light Q2 from 54.5% to 63.8%. Gains are small where the base prover already solves most (IsaPlanner 60% unaided).
agent_test: On problems needing an auxiliary fact, compare solve rate with and without a goal-directed lemma-proposal step at equal tokens; stratify by how hard the unaided baseline is.

claim: A growing library of verified lemmas gives a real but modest gain from reuse in context. LEGO-Prover: 50.4% vs 47.1% on miniF2F-valid at 50 attempts (+3.3 points), gap near zero early and widening. Conjecturing-Proving Loop: 99% (2106/2123) of its theorems re-proved with earlier library in context vs 91% (1935) with definitions only (McNemar p=4e-35).
agent_test: Run the same task stream with and without a verified-lemma store in context, same token budget; check that the gap grows with stream length.

claim: The LEGO-Prover library gain is small next to the headline and has confounds: one ablation on the valid split only, library includes trivial or duplicate lemmas (authors admit it), and 89% of skills come from the evolver, not from proof attempts. Gap search: the no-library arm also removes the evolver; 24% of 135 proved problems used retrieved skills; dedup at SequenceMatcher 0.85 exists.
agent_test: Repeat the library ablation on a held-out split and with a de-duplication and triviality filter.

claim: Separating conjecture generation from proof beats generating statement and proof together for finding a hard new theorem. Conjecturing-Proving Loop found the target in 5 of 20 runs (avg 106 theorems) vs 0 of 20 for a simple loop (avg 328), Fisher p=0.024, 14M tokens per run. One paper, one topic, one model.
agent_test: Compare a separate conjecture step plus prove step against a joint generate-and-prove step on a hard discovery task, equal tokens, 20 runs.

claim: Self-play conjecturing creates training signal when expert iteration stalls: STP proves 28.5% of LeanWorkbook vs 13.2% for expert iteration; at least 47% of generated conjectures were proved, while only 131 of 2.5M proofs of unproved statements were correct at an 11.4% checkpoint. Re-training with conjectures adds only 2-3 points on miniF2F and ProofNet at pass@128. Training result, so only the lesson (target conjectures at the edge of ability) transfers to a scaffold.
agent_test: Within one session, ask the agent to propose sub-statements of intermediate difficulty (solvable but not trivial) and measure whether solving them raises success on the main goal at equal tokens.

claim: Large conjecture pools plus decomposition give top results in formal proving: Seed-Prover heavy mode (5,000 conjectures by default, days of thinking) 121/155 past IMO problems; Hilbert recursive subgoal decomposition 99.2% miniF2F and 462/660 PutnamBench, depth ablation D=0 75% to D=2 98.36%. Different systems, stronger provers and huge compute, so the effect of lemmas alone is not isolated. Gap search: no paper holds the prover and tokens fixed; Hilbert adds a strong informal reasoner (Gemini 2.5 Pro alone 49.1%), and Seed-Prover has no lemma-pool ablation.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare decomposition into lemmas at depth 0, 1, 2 on hard items, keeping the prover fixed.

claim: Template-guided neuro-symbolic conjecturing beats pure symbolic enumeration and, at small model size, plain LLM statement writing on realistic formalisations: Lemmanaid 41.7% vs neural 38.1% on leakage-free AFP-2026; 76.6-78.9% vs 22.8% QuickSpec on Octonions. Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 with templates got 19.4% and 15.8% on AFP-2026 (direct writing 34.5% and 25.2%). One group, one gold-lemma metric.
agent_test: Offer the agent a few analogous existing lemmas as templates versus asking it to write lemmas cold; score by match to held-out gold lemmas.

claim: LLM conjecturing from a domain description works when the domain has specific structure but fails on generic algebraic laws: GPT-4 gave useful drawing-specific lemmas in about half the runs and most generic ones (associativity, commutativity) were false; renaming symbols removed the specific lemmas, which points to recall rather than derivation.
agent_test: Rename symbols in a task and check whether proposed lemmas survive; a drop signals memory, not reasoning.

claim: Early automated discovery (AM, Eurisko, Graffiti, HR) produced real results (refactorable numbers added to OEIS, many graph-theory papers) but AM's success depended on representation: concepts as small Lisp predicates mutate usefully, two-page heuristics mutated into junk. Critics found published descriptions did not match behaviour.
agent_test: Test whether mutating small, compact rules (not long plans) gives a higher useful-variant rate at equal tokens.

claim: Lemma mining from proofs gives small honest gains: 61.7% to 64.8% (about 5% relative) on core HOL Light, far below the cheating-scenario 76.5% that uses knowledge of the later proof. Evaluations that leak the lemma overstate usefulness.
agent_test: Evaluate lemma proposals only on tasks where the lemma was not derived from the answer; compare with a leak-allowed run to measure the inflation.

claim: Learning to conjecture from scratch can scale in a narrow closed domain: on 16,197 OEIS-derived problems, self-learning reached 5,565 solved vs 2,265 for CVC5/Vampire/Z3 at 60 s, but the loop took about three months and big jumps came from single reusable predicates.
agent_test: Not directly testable without training; track which stored items cause jumps in solve rate.

claim: Lemma transfer across tasks is weakly measured. Evidence is aggregate (library on vs off, in-context vs none). Only Rabe reports per-lemma reuse (used at least once inside 200,000 proofs of the same run). MathlibLemma reports 3 of 6 submitted lemmas merged but no downstream benefit. Gap search: LEGO-Prover's library is shared across problems in one run (about 32 of 135 proofs used retrieved skills), but no per-lemma cross-problem count or held-out split exists.
agent_test: Count, per stored lemma, the number of distinct later problems where it was cited in an accepted answer.

claim: Comparisons between conjecturing tools depend on benchmark and settings: TheSy was 380x faster at the 25th percentile but 1.1x slower overall than Hipster (51.6K s vs 47.1K s) because of case splitting; TheSy proves 187 of 311 vs CVC4 own conjecturing 260 on a different suite.
agent_test: None needed for the agent; keep as a caution against single-metric claims.

claim: Machine-checked verification controls bad lemmas: Hipster, MathlibLemma and CPL keep only checked proofs, MathlibLemma screens proof bypasses (sorry, axioms), and models asked in plain language about a true new theorem often judged it false (GPT-o3 always, GPT-4o 10 times).
agent_test: Require every lemma used in an answer to carry a tool-checked verification or an explicit unverified flag; measure error rate with and without.

claim: No paper compares lemma-first against longer direct attempts at equal tokens. The nearest baselines are repeated sampling with a verifier (coverage 82.9% to 98.44% on MATH, 100 to 10,000 samples) and decomposition systems that spend about 10 times the tokens (DeepSeek-Prover-V2 CoT, Hilbert 2.3M reasoner tokens per sample).
agent_test: Run lemma-first and direct arms at the same token budget with the same checker; report accuracy per token.

claim: Extra samples or tokens convert to accuracy only through a verifier. Without one, majority vote or a reward model gained under 1 point (40.50% to 41.41%) while coverage went from 82.9% to 98.44%. Models also judge counterexample rationales poorly (CounterMath strict rationale about 20-40%). So a plain-text lemma loop needs a tool check such as small-case computation.
agent_test: Add a computed small-case test to each proposed lemma before it is relied on.

claim: Retrieving existing proven theorems before proving raises accuracy and lowers cost in a decomposition system: Hilbert 99.2% vs 97.9% with reasoner tokens 2.3M vs 4.0M (Goedel-32B).
agent_test: Check known results before proposing new lemmas.

claim: The symbol-renaming recall test does not transfer to word problems (names-only change barely moves GSM8K accuracy), but perturbing constants or variables in competition problems lowers accuracy (Putnam-AXIOM: o1-preview 41.9% original, minus 19.6 points on variants). Recall of seen problems is a live reading, not proven.
agent_test: Perturb constants or domain-bearing names of a proposed lemma; a big drop signals recall.
